item.title: Staff Post - Wikiwalk Proposal
item.content:encoded:
Timer Expired. Edits made as discussed below. Author may revert at any time.

The WikiWalk team is proposing edits to this page. All proposed edits will be in a collapsible below this post, and after 7 days if there are no serious objections to the edits, the feedback received will be taken into account as the edits are made. If you have questions not directly related to the article about this project, please pm a member of the WikiWalk Team

+ Show Block
- Hide Block

Ah yes, the infamous one-way ticket SCP. A similar phenomena to this exists in SCP-3122, in which those purchasing a special GPS system find themselves going on a similarly one way trip. Given that the final line of the article leaves wiggle room for narrative expansion, an inline link there to 3122 would not be so out of place, I feel. As such, I am recommending the following edits:

Changing this:

One disturbing development: prior reports indicate that SCP-342 can only take the form of a ticket for mass transit, whereas in this case, it took on the form of a ticket for a stage play. I understand that there is a group in the Foundation that is seeking to re-open experimentation on the object in light of these new developments. Further updates as events warrant.

To this:

One disturbing development: prior reports indicate that SCP-342 can only take the form of a ticket for mass transit, whereas in this case, it took on the form of a ticket for a stage play. I understand that there is a group in the Foundation that is seeking to re-open experimentation on the object in light of these new developments. Further updates as events warrant.

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

item.content:encoded:
Of the SCPs I've read, this one has the largest gap between its quality and the number of its upvotes. This is *seriously* showing its age, and there are a number of upvotes here that I'd like to think are from people who would reconsider if they re-read it.

The idea is passable, but it doesn't remotely justify its length - particularly as most of that length is reiterating the basic information: you get on the public transport, you can't get off, you go crazy, you die/disappear. And the vast bulk of the reiteration is telling, rather than showing in an immersive manner.

The highlights are Stahm/Erin, who almost feel like characters, and the appearance of the spider was refreshing, if only as a spark of novelty in a night of repetition. But then it ends with such a glowing tribute to the deceased Dr Gunsther that it feels very much like a self-insert (and he hangs out with the senior staff at the movies, too!).

But what really gets me is the last few incident, the loss of Dr Gunsther. The calm manner to accept the inevitable, and Dr Clef frantically looking for him, it is all very well written.

However, what really gives me the creeps is the fact that it was updated 3 days ago. It gives me the feel that somewhere around this world, a doctor DID REALLY quietly and calmly accepted his fate to the doom, and his friend looking for him in despair.

The best I've read so far. Upvoted.

The "object class = containment class" is in my mind overstated, but even setting that aside, this thing has demonstrated enough challenges to warrant the Euclid designation. For one thing, it's nearly impossible to do a truly controlled test of this thing, as is demonstrated time and time again in the article.

For another, the way it targeted Dr. Gunsther suggest an unknown level of autonomy that pretty much excludes Safe. It's possible that, as Clef says, that's just melodrama, and I agree you could make a case for Safe, but it's not such a compelling one that I see any need to modify an article well over +200.

I grow more fond of this one every time i think about it. It's wordy, yeah, but that wordiness gives it strength. The core concept itself is pretty decent, but kind of simplistic (a One-way ticket…. item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I want to list out the number of reasons I like this article.

The first is the way the experiment is handled with the D-class accompanied by Strahm. I understand it's a trait of many Foundation stuff, but I always like the articles that acknowledge that for all the horrible things they've done, D-class personnel are still human beings, and that other human beings would understand that. The D-class's slow degeneration and panic makes you care about him even as you realize he was probably a horrible human being… but he was still a human being. Strahm himself thus comes off both more human and more heroic for caring about and trying to take care of his fellow human being, even though this was actually someone he could probably shoot in the head if he felt like it and would receive no more than a mild scolding. The Foundation is, in my opinion, always at its best (and best reading) when it's portrayed as being made up of real human beings rather than cold analytical science-bots.

The second is the experiment with Strahm himself and Erin. Though it's long for an SCP article, it's short for a story, and yet I still felt really attached to and invested in these characters despite the time we spend with them. It actually made me care about what happened to them and thus made what did happen really hit home, as opposed to just offhanded bland mentions with a dash of [REDACTED] which, while clinical and detached of proper style and capable of creating an oogie feeling, just can't get the same impact across. Agent █████ being dragged away while screaming and then Agent ████ drawing his service revolver because he saw [REDACTED] and was found clutching his empty revolver is kinda creepy… what actually happens there is not only creepy but heartbreaking. The emotional impact really helps the creepy along.

The following report does, I think, get a little too emotional. However if one were to assume this testing was being done in a slightly earlier time period (for some reason the idea of a bus driven by a man named Bucky makes me think of the forties or fifties… I blame this on being from the DFW metroplex, we don't really rely on what mass transit we have here to any major extent) then it makes sense, as at that time the Foundation may not have required clinical-style reports from its field agents. Just one thought to explain it. But I do think the line "Damned another person" is a little too much. Even toning it down to "doomed" or "lost" would probably work… "damned" is just too strong and specific a piece of imagery, it lets the tone overrun the events, when the events are what should be the focus.

On the other hand. That bit where the burning corpse was compelled to rise up out of the wreckage and get on the hellbus? Of sufficient horror factor to overwhelm any other problems with that section. That just sort of stirs around in your brain a bit. For some reason I can't help but imagine it as being this very calm, measured walk despite missing plenty of flesh and still on fire here and there, climbing aboard and sitting down and folding its scorched, crackling hands in its lap as the door closes and the bus drives off.

The final event is just… ow. All of it, ow. Makes me really glad I own my own car, and that we don't really go in for mass transit here. It's the sort of thing that sticks around in your brain, for sure.
